newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Euro seen needing some 'political' influence.
newsitem.headline: Euro seen needing some 'political' influence.

text.p: The European Union must ensure a "political" counterweight to the power of central banks over the planned future single currency, Portugal's Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco said on Wednesday.

Warning that the period between 1999 and 2002 could prove a time of high volatility, Sousa Franco said that the euro, the single currency, ran the risk of becoming overvalued if all decisions were left entirely in the hands of central bankers.
The first wave of countries qualifying for monetary union will lock their currencies to the euro in 1999 but their own monies will continue to exist until 2002.
"In the period of transition, financial confidence will be based on the stability and solidity of the euro," he said.
But there was a risk that this stability would come at the cost of overvaluation which could damage European companies' ability to compete.
"If the choices are only made by (a future) European Central Bank, it will always favour stability and the appreciation of the euro," Sousa Franco said.
To counter this, it would be "necessary to have a political government of Europe, a tighter coordination (of policy) up to 2002 and beyond," he said.
Sousa Franco's remarks appeared to put him firmly on the side of France in its argument with Germany over whether a future European central bank should be entirely free of all political influence.
The finance minister, who was speaking to the American Club of Lisbon, said that the euro needed to be flexible like the dollar in order not to hurt local competitivity.
Sousa Franco, a political independent who was formerly head of the country's court of accounts, said that two different concerns co-existed within Europe.

"In Germany, Austria and Holland, the fear is that the euro becomes a weak currency. In many southern countries, the risk is that the euro could come to be so strong that it threatens their ability to compete," he said.
But in Portugal, there was more of "a culture of stability than people think," he added.
The fact that the years between 1999 and 2002 could be volatile meant that it might be better to try to shorten the period of transition, the minister said.
"The period is too long. It would be good if it could be reduced," he said.
He said the future single currency was likely to have a far greater weight in world trade than the combined role of European currencies today.
Between 2002 and 2005, it could account for some 30 percent of international currency flows compared with the 15 to 20 percent covered by European currencies at present.
